<!-- llms-index: https://docs.gradle.com/develocity/llms.txt -->

# Develocity Reporting via Amazon Athena Installation Manual

<a id="preamble"></a>

You are viewing the documentation for Athena Data Export version 2.0. Users still utilizing version 1.0 can find its manual at the following [Develocity Reporting via Amazon Athena Installation Manual 1.0](https://docs.gradle.com/develocity/legacy/reporting-aws/installation-manual/1.0/).

<a id="introduction"></a>

## Introduction

This guide provides instructions for visualizing Develocity build data in Grafana dashboards by exporting the build data as build models to Amazon S3 and querying them via Amazon Athena as part of DRV 2.0.

> [!NOTE]
> If you want to visualize Develocity build data without using AWS services, you can install the Develocity Reporting Kit.

<a id="build-data"></a>

### Build Data

A Build Scan® is a persisted record of a single build’s captured data. Each Build Scan consists of thousands to millions of very fine-grained events. Build models aggregate these events into higher-level structures to expose easily consumable, summarized information about the build.

The build models can be exported to Amazon S3 to serve as input to an external big data engine, and they can be consumed via the [Develocity API](https://docs.gradle.com/develocity/2026.2/reference/develocity-api/). This guide focuses on exporting the build models to [Amazon S3](https://aws.amazon.com/s3/) and their consumption by [Amazon Athena](https://aws.amazon.com/athena/).

The build models that are available to DRV are served by the [`builds` endpoint of the Develocity API](https://docs.gradle.com/develocity/2026.2/reference/develocity-api/#reference_documentation).

> [!NOTE]
> All builds exported to S3 via the Athena Data Export functionality are subject to the same retention period that’s configured for Develocity

<a id="upgrading-from-v1-0"></a>

### Upgrading From V1.0

For any customers that are currently using Athena V1.0 via the Build Model Export feature and wishing to upgrade, please follow the upgrade instructions in [Appendix E](#v1_upgrade_guide)

<a id="upgrading-from-develocity-earlier-than-2025-3"></a>

### Upgrading From Develocity Earlier Than 2025.3

Customers already using the Athena Data Export feature and plan to upgrade to Develocity 2025.3 or later should follow the instructions in [Appendix F](#upgrade_guide_2_0) to ensure a smooth transition to the new _synchronized Athena Data Export_ process.

<a id="setup"></a>

## Setup

The process for setting up the infrastructure at a high level is as follows:

1.  [Create a database](#configure_aws_glue) in AWS Glue containing the table of the build models.
    
2.  [Create a workgroup](#create_athena_workgroup) in Amazon Athena to query the table with the build models.
    
3.  [Configure the AWS permissions](#configure_aws_permissions) required for the Athena Data Export process to run.
    
4.  [Set up the build model schema](#create_athena_schema) in Amazon Athena.
    
5.  [Enable Athena Data Export](#enable_v2_data_export) in Develocity to populate and optimize the raw data.
    
6.  [Verify the Athena Data Export process](#verify_athena_setup) by issuing a build model query from Amazon Athena.
    
7.  [Create a data source](#configure_grafana) in Grafana for the table you created in Amazon Athena.
    
8.  [Create a Grafana dashboard](#create_dashboard) that visualizes data from the build models.
    
9.  [Import the Grafana dashboards](#import_dashboards) provided by Gradle.
    

In the following steps, we will outline how each step can be completed.

<a id="prerequisites"></a>

### Prerequisites

The prerequisites are as follows:

*   A Develocity account with the _Configure access control_ and _Configure operational settings_ [permissions](https://docs.gradle.com/develocity/2026.2/administration/access-control/permissions-and-roles/) (just _Administer Develocity_ on pre-2025.4 Develocity instances) for configuring Develocity.
    
*   An Amazon S3 location to store the exported data
    
*   An AWS account with permissions to configure Amazon Athena and AWS Glue.
    
*   A Grafana instance (on-premise or cloud) with the [Athena plugin](https://grafana.com/grafana/plugins/grafana-athena-datasource/?tab=installation) installed.
    

<a id="configure_aws_glue"></a>

### Configure AWS Glue

Athena uses Glue to store the table schema. To create a database inside the data catalog, follow the Glue instructions at [Working with databases on the AWS Glue console](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/glue/latest/dg/define-database.html).

This guide assumes the created database is named `develocity-db`, but you may choose a different name.

<a id="configure_aws_athena"></a>

### Configure Amazon Athena

Create an Athena workgroup and table to build models from Develocity. You will need the [AmazonAthenaFullAccess managed policy](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/athena/latest/ug/managed-policies.html#amazonathenafullaccess-managed-policy) to perform these tasks.

<a id="create_athena_workgroup"></a>

#### Create an Amazon Athena Workgroup

An Athena workgroup is required to define the parameters for running queries against the build models. To create an Athena workgroup, follow the Athena instructions at [Create a workgroup](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/athena/latest/ug/creating-workgroups.html).

In step 5, do the following:

1.  Choose **Athena SQL** as the engine type.
    
2.  Specify a new folder in your S3 bucket to store Athena’s query results in **Location of query result** on the **Query result configuration** pane.
    
    ![Example of the Athena Query Result Configuration Pane](https://docs.gradle.com/develocity/reporting-aws/2.1/_images/query-result-config.png)
    
    Example of the Athena Query Result Configuration Pane
    

This guide assumes the query results folder is named `query-results` in an S3 bucket named `develocity` and the created workgroup is named `develocity-wg`, but you may choose different names.

> [!TIP]
> Pay attention to AWS’ suggestions for lifecycle configuration. Resource usage and costs may increase significantly if this isn’t configured.

<a id="configure_aws_permissions"></a>

### Configure AWS Permissions

The [AmazonAthenaFullAccess managed policy](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/athena/latest/ug/managed-policies.html#amazonathenafullaccess-managed-policy) covers all the required permissions for any credentials that the Athena Data Export process and related features will make use of.

However in cases where the granted permissions are too broad, the minimal permissions required for the Athena Data Export process are as described below.

> [!NOTE]
> These are additional permissions required for using the Athena Data Export process. Any existing S3 permissions set up for Develocity are still required.

```json
{
	"Version": "2012-10-17",
	"Statement": [
		{
			"Effect": "Allow",
			"Action": [
				"s3:GetBucketLocation",
				"s3:GetObject",
				"s3:DeleteObject",
				"s3:ListBucket",
				"s3:ListBucketMultipartUploads",
				"s3:ListMultipartUploadParts",
				"s3:AbortMultipartUpload",
				"s3:CreateBucket",
				"s3:PutObject",
				"s3:PutBucketPublicAccessBlock"
			],
			"Resource": [
				"arn:aws:s3:::${name.of.bucket}", (1)
				"arn:aws:s3:::${name.of.bucket}/*" (1)
			]
		},
		{
			"Effect": "Allow",
			"Action": [
				"athena:GetQueryExecution",
				"athena:GetQueryResults",
				"athena:GetQueryResultsStream",
				"athena:GetWorkGroup",
				"athena:StartQueryExecution",
				"athena:StopQueryExecution"
			],
			"Resource": [
              "arn:aws:athena:*:*:workgroup/${name.of.workgroup}" (2)
			]
		},
		{
			"Effect": "Allow",
			"Action": [
				"glue:GetDatabase",
				"glue:GetDatabases",
				"glue:GetTable",
				"glue:GetTables",
				"glue:GetPartitions",
				"glue:GetPartition",
				"glue:BatchCreatePartition",
				"glue:BatchDeletePartition",
				"glue:CreateDatabase",  (3)
				"glue:CreateTable",  (3)
				"glue:UpdateTable",  (3)
				"glue:DeleteTable"  (3)
			],
			"Resource": [
				"arn:aws:glue:*:*:catalog", (4)
				"arn:aws:glue:*:*:database/${name.of.glue.db}", (4)
				"arn:aws:glue:*:*:table/${name.of.glue.db}/*" (4)
			]
		},
		{
			"Effect": "Allow",
			"Action": [
				"athena:ListDatabases"
			],
			"Resource": [
				"*"
			]
		}
	]
}
```

1. ARN of the S3 bucket used to store the results. Replace ${name.of.bucket} with the value used in the ${s3.path} placeholder when setting up the DDL.
2. ARN of the created workgroup. Replace ${name.of.workgroup} with the Athena workgroup created earlier, assumed to be develocity-wg.
3. These permissions are only required if you are using the automatic schema management feature, and can be excluded if the feature is disabled.
4. ARN of the Glue database and tables. The resources are of the following pattern (replace ${name.of.glue.db} with the database name created earlier, assumed to be develocity-db):

```
${arn:partition:service:region:account-id}:catalog
${arn:partition:service:region:account-id}:database/${name.of.glue.db}
${arn:partition:service:region:account-id}:table/${name.of.glue.db}
```

<a id="create_athena_schema"></a>

### Set Up the Athena Schema

The Athena Data Export process requires a schema to be set up in Amazon Athena to make the stored build models queryable. This schema describes the structure of the build models and how they’re stored in S3. Starting from Develocity version 2025.3, Develocity will automatically create and manage all the schema, views and tables required for the Athena Data Export process to function. For more information on this, see [Automatic Schema Management](#automatic_schema_management). For users that prefer to manage the schema themselves, the steps to take are described in [Appendix D](#athena_user_managed_schema).

> [!NOTE]
> Although using the default automatic schema management is recommended for a smoother experience, it isn’t required to use the Athena Data Export process. See Appendix D for details on how to set up a user-managed schema.

<a id="enable_v2_data_export"></a>

### Enabling Athena Data Export in Develocity

<a id="s3-object-storage-configuration"></a>

#### S3 Object Storage Configuration

Before you can enable the Athena Data Export process, you need to ensure that Develocity has access to an S3 bucket to store the exported _build models_ so that they’re accessible by Athena. The following configuration block of the `values.yaml` Helm chart demonstrates the minimal configuration to enable object storage in S3.

```yaml
objectStorage:
  type: s3
  s3:
    bucket: develocity
    region: «aws-region»
    credentials:
      source: configuration
      accessKey: "«aws-access-key»"
      secretKey: "«aws-secret-key»"
```

> [!NOTE]
> You don’t need to store your Build Scan data in S3 to export the build models to S3.

Please refer to the “Amazon S3” section in the [Standalone Helm Chart Configuration Guide](https://docs.gradle.com/develocity/2026.2/reference/helm-charts/standalone/#object_storage_s3) or the [Kubernetes Helm Chart Configuration Guide](https://docs.gradle.com/develocity/2026.2/reference/helm-charts/cluster/#object_storage_s3) for more information on configuring S3 object storage.

<a id="athena-data-export-configuration"></a>

#### Athena Data Export Configuration

You can enable the Athena Data Export by setting the appropriate values in your Develocity `values.yaml`, which can be obtained from the setup done so far.

```yaml
athenaDataExport:
  enabled: true
  workgroup: $WORKGROUP (1)
  region: $REGION (2)
  catalog: AwsDataCatalog
  database: $DATABASE (3)
  credentials:
    type: (4)
    irsa:
      serviceAccountAnnotations: (5)
    keys:
      accessKey: (6)
      secretKey: (6)
      secretName: (6)
```

1. The name of the workgroup you created in Amazon Athena (assumed to be develocity-wg)
2. The AWS region where the workgroup is located.
3. The name of the Glue database you created (assumed to be develocity-db).
4. Must be one of irsa / instanceProfile / keys
5. Can only be set if irsa is set as the credentials type. For more details on IRSA refer to IAM roles for service account.
6. Can only be set if keys is set as the credentials type. Either accessKey and secretKey must be set with the AWS access key and secret key, or else a secretName provided which references the name of a Kubernetes secret containing accessKey and secretKey keys.

<a id="automatic_schema_management"></a>

#### Automatic Schema Management

Enabled by default, Develocity will automatically create and manage the schema required for the Athena Data Export process to function. This allows for a smoother experience when setting up the Athena Data Export process, as well as keeping the schema up to date in future releases. For some customers, however, this may not be desirable. This could be due to organizational policies that require strict control over changes to the schema.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> Develocity will only manage the schema for the new synchronized Athena Data Export process introduced in version 2025.3. If you choose to use the legacy one-off Athena Data Export process, or you keep running it alongside the new synchronized Athena Data Export process, you will need to manage the schema for the legacy one-off Athena Data Export process yourself. To manage the schema manually you can follow the steps in Appendix D.

To disable automatic schema management, add the following property to your Develocity `values.yaml`:

```yaml
athenaDataExport:
  schemaManagement:
    enabled: false
```

By default the automatic schema management is using the same credentials as the Athena Data Export process itself. This can be overridden by specifying a different set of credentials for the schema management process:

```yaml
athenaDataExport:
  schemaManagement:
    enabled: true
    credentials: (1)
      type: (2)
      irsa:
        serviceAccountAnnotations: (3)
      keys:
        accessKey: (4)
        secretKey: (4)
        secretName: (4)
```

1. Optional: the credentials to use for automated schema management. Since the automatic schema management process requires broader permissions, this allows you to minimize the permissions granted to the Athena Data Export process. See Configure AWS permissions for more details.
2. If specified, must be one of irsa / instanceProfile / keys
3. Can only be set if irsa is set as the credentials type. For more details on IRSA refer to IAM roles for service account.
4. Can only be set if keys is set as the credentials type. Either accessKey and secretKey must be set with the AWS access key and secret key, or else a secretName provided which references the name of a Kubernetes secret containing accessKey and secretKey keys.

This will also ensure that the schema will be kept up to date in future releases, should there be any changes to the schema.

<a id="verify_athena_setup"></a>

### Verify the Amazon Athena Setup

Run a simple query against the `build` table to verify that the Athena Data Export process is properly set up and connected to AWS.

In the [Query Editor](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/athena/latest/ug/step-3-query-data.html), select the database you created in Glue and issue a simple build model query:

```sql
SELECT COUNT(*) AS "Build Count last 7 days"
FROM build
WHERE build_start_date BETWEEN CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '7' DAY AND CURRENT_DATE
```

> [!TIP]
> The `build_start_date` column is a partition key in the table, and queries that filter on this column will be more efficient.

The results are displayed in a table below the Query Editor:

![Example of Verifying the Amazon Athena Setup in the Query Editor](https://docs.gradle.com/develocity/reporting-aws/2.1/_images/athena-test-query.png)

Example of Verifying the Amazon Athena Setup in the Query Editor

<a id="configure_grafana"></a>

### Configure Grafana

This requires a Grafana instance (on-premise or cloud) with the [Athena plugin](https://grafana.com/grafana/plugins/grafana-athena-datasource/) installed.

<a id="connect_to_athena"></a>

#### Connect to Amazon Athena

Add a data source pointing to your Glue database and Athena table. To create a data source, follow the Grafana instructions at [Configure the data source in Grafana](https://grafana.com/grafana/plugins/grafana-athena-datasource/?tab=installation).

In step 2, do the following:

1.  Enter your AWS credentials and default region in **Connection Details** (see the [Athena plugin for Grafana](https://grafana.com/grafana/plugins/grafana-athena-datasource/) documentation for the different authentication options).
    
2.  Select **AWSDataCatalog** from **Data source**.
    
3.  Select the database you created in Glue from **Database**.
    
4.  Select the workgroup you created in Athena from **Workgroup**.
    
5.  Leave **Output Location** empty to use your workgroup’s default output location.
    
6.  Click **Save & test**.
    
    ![Example of Adding Athena as a Datasource to Grafana](https://docs.gradle.com/develocity/reporting-aws/2.1/_images/connect-grafana-athena.png)
    
    Example of Adding Athena as a Datasource to Grafana
    

> [!TIP]
> If you use Grafana Cloud and choose to provide authorization using the AWS Assume Role feature, note that this feature is in private preview. You must contact technical support at Grafana to enable it for your stack.

See [Grafana data sources](https://grafana.com/docs/grafana-cloud/connect-externally-hosted/data-sources/) for more information.

<a id="create_dashboard"></a>

### Create a Dashboard

Create a Grafana dashboard that displays Develocity build data in a chart. To create a dashboard, follow the Grafana instructions at [Create a dashboard](https://grafana.com/docs/grafana-cloud/visualizations/dashboards/build-dashboards/create-dashboard/).

In step four, select the Grafana data source you previously created from **Data source**.

The following image shows a bar chart visualization of the number of builds grouped by day using the following query:

```sql
SELECT count(DISTINCT id), build_start_date
FROM build
WHERE $__dateFilter(build_start_date) (1)
GROUP BY build_start_date
```

1. The $__dateFilter macro is provided by the Athena data source and is used to inject the time range selected in the Grafana dashboard as a filter criterion of the query.

![Example of a Dashboard Showing a Bar Chart Visualization of the Number of Builds Grouped by Day](https://docs.gradle.com/develocity/reporting-aws/2.1/_images/example-dashboard.png)

Example of a Dashboard Showing a Bar Chart Visualization of the Number of Builds Grouped by Day

See [Grafana dashboards](https://grafana.com/docs/grafana-cloud/visualizations/dashboards/) for more information.

<a id="import_dashboards"></a>

### Import the Gradle-Provided Dashboards

Gradle provides a set of pre-defined, JSON-based Develocity dashboard definitions. Contact your technical contact from Develocity for assistance integrating them into your on-premise or cloud Grafana instance.

The dashboard bundle can be downloaded from [Dashboard Bundle Downloads](#dashboard_downloads).

The required steps to import the dashboards provided by Gradle differ depending on the type of Grafana installation. Besides the manual import of dashboards and the simple built-in [provisioning mechanism](https://grafana.com/docs/grafana/latest/administration/provisioning/#dashboards), Grafana also provides a [variety](https://grafana.com/docs/grafana-cloud/as-code/infrastructure-as-code/) of _Infrastructure as Code_ options to manage dashboards.

<a id="dashboards_compatibility"></a>

#### Compatibility

<a id="grafana"></a>

##### Grafana

See [Grafana dashboard compatibility](https://docs.gradle.com/develocity/2026.2/miscellaneous/compatibility/#develocity_reporting_and_visualization_grafana).

<a id="build-environment"></a>

##### Build Environment

Most of the Gradle-provided dashboards rely on the presence of specific [tags](https://docs.gradle.com/develocity/gradle/4.5/gradle-plugin/#adding_tags) and [custom values](https://docs.gradle.com/develocity/gradle/4.5/gradle-plugin/#adding_custom_values) on Build Scans to render the desired visualizations.

Tags used within the dashboards:

1.  `CI` - Used throughout the dashboards to classify builds as either CI (tag is present) or local (tag is absent) builds
    

Custom values used within the dashboards:

1.  `Git repository` - The URI of the Git repository that the build was run in, for example, `git@github.com:gradle/gradle.git`
    
2.  `CI provider` - The name of the CI provider that ran the build, for example, `GitHub Actions`
    

> [!TIP]
> If you are using the Common Custom User Data Gradle plugin or Common Custom User Data Maven extension, this information will be automatically added to every Build Scan.

<a id="import_prerequisites"></a>

#### Prerequisites

This section requires a downloaded and unzipped [dashboard bundle](#dashboard_downloads).

> [!NOTE]
> Throughout the following steps, all shell commands are expected to be run in the root directory of the extracted dashboard bundle.

You must insert the `UID` of your Grafana Athena datasource into the dashboard JSON files. You can use the following command to globally insert the UID into all JSON files:

```shell
find ./dashboards -type f -name '*.json' -exec sed -i.bak 's/athena-datasource-uid-placeholder/YOUR-DATASOURCE-UID/g' {} \; \
    && find ./dashboards -type f -name '*.json.bak' -exec rm {} \;
```

> [!TIP]
> You can find your datasource’s UID in the Grafana UI by navigating to Connections → Data Sources and clicking on the Athena datasource. The UID is displayed in the URL.

<a id="grafana-installation-types"></a>

#### Grafana Installation Types

<a id="grafana_provisioning"></a>

##### Using Grafana’s Built-in Provisioning Mechanism

**Use if** you have access to the file system of the Grafana server.

Grafana has a [provisioning mechanism](https://grafana.com/docs/grafana/latest/administration/provisioning/#dashboards) that allows you to point it to a directory containing dashboard definitions in JSON format. Grafana will then watch that directory for changes and automatically import new dashboards or update existing ones.

**Steps:**

1.  Replace the datasource UID placeholder in the dashboard files with the Athena datasource UID from your installation as described in [prerequisites](#import_prerequisites).
    
2.  Copy the contents of the `dashboards` folder from the provided zip file within into a directory on your Grafana server. This guide assumes you copied the contents into `/var/lib/grafana/dashboards` so that you end up with the following directory structure:
    
    ```
    /var/lib/grafana/dashboards/
    ├─ 00 - Overview/
    │  ├─ global-volume.json
    │  ├─ project-volume.json
    ├─ 10 - Environment/
    │  ├─ build-tools.json
    │  ├─ ...
    ├─ ...
    ```
    
3.  Place a `dashboards.yaml` file with the following content into Grafana’s provisioning directory at `/etc/grafana/provisioning/dashboards/`.
    
    ```yaml
    apiVersion: 1
    providers:
      - name: 'Gradle Develocity Dashboards'
        type: file
        allowUiUpdates: false
        disableDeletion: true
        updateIntervalSeconds: 60
        options:
          path: /var/lib/grafana/dashboards
          foldersFromFilesStructure: true
    ```
    

<a id="grafana_provisioning_helm"></a>

##### Using Grafana’s Provisioning Mechanism With Helm and Kubernetes

**Use if** you are self-hosting Grafana in a Kubernetes cluster and you manage your Grafana deployment with Helm.

The Grafana Helm chart contains an option that allows Grafana to discover and collect dashboards stored in ConfigMaps within the cluster.

**Steps:**

1.  Replace the datasource UID placeholder in the dashboard files with the Athena datasource UID from your installation as described in [prerequisites](#import_prerequisites).
    
2.  Place the dashboards into ConfigMaps with the label `grafana_dashboard: "1"`. Grafana recommends creating one ConfigMap per dashboard. You can create ConfigMaps individually per dashboard using the following `kubectl` command:
    
    ```shell
    kubectl create configmap overview-global-volume-dashboard \
            -n <YOUR-NAMESPACE> \
            --from-file='./dashboards/00 - Overview/global-volume.json' \
            --dry-run=client \
            -o yaml \
        | kubectl label -f- --dry-run=client -o yaml --local grafana_dashboard=1 \
        | kubectl annotate -f- --dry-run=client -o yaml --local 'grafana_folder=/tmp/dashboards/00 - Overview' \
        | kubectl apply --server-side=true -f -
    ```
    
    To help you with importing all our dashboards, preserving the recommended folder structure, we’ve prepared a kustomize file along with the dashboard bundle. It can be applied with this command:
    
    ```shell
    kubectl kustomize ./ | kubectl apply -n <YOUR-NAMESPACE> --server-side=true -f -
    ```
    
3.  Enable and configure the `dashboards` sidecar container in Grafana’s `values.yaml` file:
    
    ```yaml
    sidecar:
      dashboards:
        enabled: true
        label: grafana_dashboard
        label_value: '1'
        folderAnnotation: grafana_folder
        provider:
          name: 'Gradle Develocity Dashboards'
          type: file
          allowUiUpdates: false
          disableDeletion: true
          foldersFromFilesStructure: true
    ```
    
    For more information, refer to Grafana’s [Helm installation guide](https://grafana.com/docs/grafana/latest/setup-grafana/installation/helm/) and the [Helm Chart documentation](https://github.com/grafana/helm-charts/tree/main/charts/grafana).
    

<a id="grafana_manual_import"></a>

##### Manually Importing Dashboards via the Grafana UI

**Use if** you only need a small subset of the provided dashboards, and you can not use any of the more automated methods described above.

> [!NOTE]
> You need to have the `Editor` role in Grafana to import dashboards via the UI.

**Steps**

1.  Replace the datasource UID placeholder in the dashboard files with the Athena datasource UID from your installation as described in [prerequisites](#import_prerequisites).
    
2.  Go to your Grafana’s dashboard view at `[https://your-grafana-instance.com/dashboards](https://your-grafana-instance.com/dashboards)`.
    
3.  Optional: Create a new folder for the Gradle dashboards by clicking on the `New` button and selecting `Create Folder` from the dropdown.
    
4.  Click the `New` button and select `Import`.
    
5.  Drag and drop the JSON file of the dashboard you want to import into the drop zone or click on the drop zone to open a file dialog, then click `Load`.
    
6.  Confirm the name of the dashboard and the folder you want to import it into and click `Import`.
    

<a id="grafana_terraform_aws"></a>

##### Using Amazon Managed Grafana With Terraform

**Use if** you want to use Amazon Managed Grafana, and you manage your infrastructure with Terraform.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> This only deploys the Amazon Managed Grafana instance and imports the dashboards. This requires an already working Athena setup to succeed. Amazon Managed Grafana uses either AWS IAM Identity Center or SAML. The provided terraform scripts only support IAM Identity Center. If you want to use SAML adjust the terraform modules in terraform/modules/develocity-drv-aws-grafana-athena/grafana.tf accordingly.

As part of our dashboard bundle, we provide a set of terraform modules and scripts alongside it to create and populate an Amazon Managed Grafana instance along with the required permissions, buckets, and other ancillary resources. These modules are placed in the `terraform/modules` directory and can be integrated into your existing infrastructure as a code pipeline.

> [!TIP]
> In the following steps we provide a set of shell scripts to execute a deployment of the Amazon Managed Grafana instance. These scripts are provided as a convenience and can be used as a reference to integrate the terraform modules into your existing infrastructure as code pipeline.

**Steps**

*   Ensure you have the AWS CLI installed and configured using the necessary [permissions](#permissions).
    
*   Make sure you have Terraform installed.
    
*   **Decompress the provided dashboard bundle and navigate to the `terraform` directory. Every subsequent step should be executed in this directory**.
    
*   In the `terraform` directory, there are three shell scripts that are used in the subsequent steps to deploy the Amazon Managed Grafana instance:
    
*   `provision-grafana.sh`: to deploy the Amazon Managed Grafana instance and its required resources.
    
*   `provision-grafana-datasources.sh`: to install the Athena plugin and create the Athena datasource.
    
*   `provision-drv-dashboards.sh`: to import the dashboards.
    

<a id="prepare_environment"></a>

###### Prepare Your Environment

```shell
unzip gradle-dashboards-bundle-X-X-X.zip
```

Change your working directory to the unzipped dashboard bundle:

```shell
cd terraform
```

<a id="provision_grafana"></a>

###### Provision the Amazon Managed Grafana Instance

> [!IMPORTANT]
> The provided modules assumes using AWS Identity Center to manage the users and groups that have access to the Amazon Managed Grafana instance. In this case, a set of user/group SSO IDs are required to set up the Grafana instance. These IDs aren’t the same as AWS user IDs. They need to be retrieved from the AWS SSO console. Please contact your AWS SSO administrator to get these IDs.

Run the `provision-grafana.sh` script to deploy the Amazon Managed Grafana instance and its required resources.

```shell
provision-grafana.sh \
    --bucket-name develocity \(1)
    --aws-region eu-west-1 \(2)
    --aws-profile my-profile \(3)
    --develocity-drv-grafana-admin-user-ids my-sso-id \(4)
    --develocity-drv-grafana-admin-group-ids my-sso-id \(4)
    --prefix develocity \(5)
    --apply \ (6)
    --destroy (6)
```

1. The bucket name where your build models are stored. This is usually the same as the bucket as the one configured for Develocity.
2. The region where you want to deploy the Amazon Managed Grafana instance.
3. The name of the AWS CLI profile you want to use to deploy the resources.
4. The SSO IDs of the groups or users you want to have admin access to the Grafana instance. This is a repeatable argument. At least one of these arguments must be provided.
5. An optional prefix for the resources created by the script. This is useful to avoid naming conflicts when deploying to the same AWS account.
6. To apply or destroy the resources respectively. If neither is provided, the script will default to creating a terraform plan. In either of these cases you will still need to interactively approve the plan before application.

<a id="provision_grafana_datasources"></a>

###### Install the Athena Plugin and Create the Athena Datasource

Once the Amazon Managed Grafana instance is deployed, you can then install the Athena plugin and create the Athena datasource by running `provision-grafana-datasources.sh`:

```shell
provision-grafana-datasources.sh \
    --db-name develocity-db \(1)
    --grafana-URL https://my-grafana-URL.com \(2)
    --grafana-token my-grafana-token \(3)
    --workgroup develocity-wg \(4)
    --aws-region eu-west-1 \(5)
    --apply \(6)
    --destroy (6)
```

1. The name of the Glue database where the Athena tables were created.
2. Optional parameter, normally provided by the previous script automatically The URL of the Amazon Managed Grafana instance.
3. Optional parameter, normally provided by the previous script automatically The API token for the Amazon Managed Grafana instance.
4. Optional parameter, normally provided by the previous script automatically The name of the Athena workgroup.
5. Optional parameter, normally provided by the previous script automatically The region where the Amazon Managed Grafana instance was deployed.
6. To apply or destroy the resources respectively. If neither is provided, the script will default to creating a terraform plan. In both cases you will still need to interactively approve the plan before application.

<a id="import_dashboards_to_managed_grafana"></a>

###### Import the Provided Dashboards

Finally, you can import the dashboards to the provisioned Grafana instance by running `provision-drv-dashboards.sh`:

```shell
provision-drv-dashboards.sh \
    --dashboard-folder-path ../../../dashboards \(1)
    --grafana-URL https://my-grafana-URL.com \(2)
    --grafana-token my-grafana-token \(3)
    --datasource-id my-datasource-id \(4)
    --apply \(5)
    --destroy (5)
```

1. The path to the directory containing the dashboard JSON files. If you are using the provided dashboard bundle this will be ../dashboards.
2. Optional parameter, normally provided by the previous script automatically The URL of the Amazon Managed Grafana instance.
3. Optional parameter, normally provided by the previous script automatically The API token for the Amazon Managed Grafana instance.
4. Optional parameter, normally provided by the previous script automatically The ID of the datasource created in the previous stage.
5. To apply or destroy the resources respectively. If none is provided the script will default to create a terraform plan. In either of these cases you will still need to interactively approve the plan before application.

> [!TIP]
> For security reasons, the lifetime of the Grafana token used to configure the Amazon Managed Grafana instance is limited. If the token expires, you will receive Access denied errors from AWS when applying the Terraform plans. To fix this, you can rerun the provision-grafana-datasources.sh script with the --apply flag to generate a new token. This won’t affect any of the previously deployed resources.

If the script executions fail for some reason, the commands `terraform output stages/stage_name` can be used to get the outputs of the executed stage. This should provide valuable information to investigate the failures alongside with the Grafana URL and the administrator token.

<a id="permissions"></a>

Deploying an Amazon Managed Grafana instance requires many permissions because it’s a complex operation involving several resource types. The list of permissions and AWS-managed policies that need to be attached to the user/role executing the terraform scripts is shown below:

*   Permissions required for managing IAM resources
    
    *   These permissions are required to manage the role that can be assumed by the managed Grafana instance, which has access to the bucket storing the build-model data used by Athena.
        
    *   `iam:ListRoles`
        
    *   `iam:CreateRole`
        
    *   `iam:GetRole`
        
    *   `iam:DeleteRole`
        
    *   `iam:ListRolePolicies`
        
    *   `iam:ListAttachedRolePolicies`
        
    *   `iam:ListInstanceProfilesForRole`
        
    *   `iam:AttachRolePolicy`
        
    *   `iam:PutRolePolicy`
        
    *   `iam:GetRolePolicy`
        
    *   `iam:DeleteRolePolicy`
        
    *   `iam:DetachRolePolicy`
        
    
*   AWS managed policy required to manage S3 connections
    
    *   This policy is required to be able to create and manage a bucket that will store the query results executed by Athena.
        
    *   `AmazonS3FullAccess`
        
    
*   AWS managed policy required to manage Athena resources
    
    *   This policy is required to be able to create and manage the Athena workgroup and the Athena database.
        
    *   `AmazonAthenaFullAccess`
        
    
*   AWS managed policy required to administer the Amazon Managed Grafana instance
    
    *   This policy is required to be able to create and manage the Amazon Managed Grafana instance.
        
    *   `AWSGrafanaAccountAdministrator`
        
    
*   AWS managed policies to manage the SSO settings
    
    *   These policies are required to manage the SSO settings for the Amazon Managed Grafana instance.
        
    *   `AWSOrganizationsFullAccess`
        
    *   `AWSSSODirectoryAdministrator`
        
    *   `AWSSSOMasterAccountAdministrator`
        
    

<a id="upgrading"></a>

## Upgrading

<a id="upgrading-athena-tables"></a>

### Upgrading Athena Tables

After 2025.3, Develocity will automatically manage the schema required for the Athena Data Export process to function. If you are using the automatic schema management, no action is required to upgrade the Athena tables.

When upgrading Develocity, the schema of the build models may change, and existing views may be updated to include new data to be consumed via the dashboards. This would require updating the Athena tables and views to reflect the new schema.

The automatic schema management will follow the process outlined below to upgrade the tables as needed. All data queried by Athena is stored in external tables or views. Both of these constructs don’t store any data themselves but rather point to the location of the data, that ultimately resides in S3 buckets. This means there is no data loss when dropping the tables or views.

As such, upgrading the Athena tables is a simple process of dropping the tables and views, and re-creating them with the new schema. The same steps as in the [initial setup](#create_athena_schema) can be followed, but with the updated schema files downloaded from the [dashboard bundle](#dashboard_downloads).

<a id="upgrading-grafana-dashboards"></a>

### Upgrading Grafana Dashboards

When upgrading Develocity, as new data becomes available, new dashboards may be created to surface more insights. To upgrade the Grafana dashboards, follow these steps:

> [!IMPORTANT]
> This will delete every dashboard on your Grafana. If you have created new ones or have imported the dashboards to a Grafana that has other dashboards, make sure to only remove the dashboards supplied by Gradle.

Deploying the new set of dashboards depends on how it was originally installed/provisioned. Therefore, please follow the appropriate instructions for your Grafana installation type.

<a id="upgrade-dashboards-via-built-in-provisioning"></a>

#### Upgrade Dashboards via Built-in Provisioning

If you have followed the procedure of [importing the dashboards via Grafana provisioning](#grafana_provisioning), you can follow these steps to upgrade the dashboards:

1.  Open your Grafana provisioning folder.
    
2.  Delete all folders and files you want to update within the folder.
    
    *   In a Docker desktop environment, this may cause Docker to stop syncing changes, so you may need to restart the container, or delete the files one by one, or enable `File Sharing` in your Docker Desktop settings.
        
    
3.  Open your Grafana and log in with a user account with edit privileges.
    
4.  Open the Dashboards view and select the checkbox next to the `Name` header to select all folders.  
    
    ![Example of Selecting All Dashboard Folders by Name](https://docs.gradle.com/develocity/reporting-aws/2.1/_images/delete_dashboards.png)
    
    Example of Selecting All Dashboard Folders by Name
    
5.  Click **Delete**, this will remove all dangling folders from the Grafana UI that cannot be automatically unprovisioned.
    
6.  Download the latest [dashboard bundle](#dashboard_downloads).
    
7.  Replace the datasource UID placeholder in the dashboard files with the Athena datasource UID from your installation as described in prerequisites.
    
8.  Copy the contents of the dashboards folder from the provided zip file within into a directory on your Grafana server.
    
9.  Restart your Grafana instance to apply the changes.
    

<a id="grafana_helm"></a>

#### Upgrade Dashboards via Helm and Kubernetes Provisioning

If you have followed the procedure of [importing the dashboards via Grafana provisioning with Helm and Kubernetes](#grafana_provisioning_helm), you can follow these steps to upgrade the dashboards:

1.  Delete the ConfigMaps containing the dashboards.
    
    ```shell
    kubectl --namespace <YOUR-NAMESPACE> delete configmap -l grafana_dashboard=1
    ```
    
2.  Open your Grafana and log in with a user account with edit privileges.
    
3.  Open the Dashboards view and click the checkbox next to the `Name` header to select all folders.  
    
    ![Example of Selecting All Dashboard Folders by Name](https://docs.gradle.com/develocity/reporting-aws/2.1/_images/delete_dashboards.png)
    
    Example of Selecting All Dashboard Folders by Name
    
4.  Click **Delete**.
    
5.  Download the latest [dashboard bundle](#dashboard_downloads).
    
6.  Replace the datasource UID placeholder in the dashboard files with the Athena datasource UID from your installation as described in prerequisites.
    
7.  Run the provided kustomize file to re-import the dashboards.
    
    ```shell
    kubectl kustomize ./ | kubectl apply -n <YOUR-NAMESPACE> --server-side=true -f -
    ```
    

<a id="upgrading-manually-imported-dashboards"></a>

#### Upgrading Manually Imported Dashboards

If you have followed the procedure of [manually importing the dashboards](#grafana_manual_import), you can follow these steps to upgrade the dashboards:

1.  Open your Grafana and log in with a user account with edit privileges.
    
2.  Open the Dashboards view and click the checkbox next to the `Name` header to select all folders.  
    
    ![Example of Selecting All Dashboard Folders by Name](https://docs.gradle.com/develocity/reporting-aws/2.1/_images/delete_dashboards.png)
    
    Example of Selecting All Dashboard Folders by Name
    
3.  Click **Delete**.
    
4.  Download the latest [dashboard bundle](#dashboard_downloads) and follow the installation procedure as previously.
    

<a id="upgrading-aws-managed-grafana-installed-with-terraform"></a>

#### Upgrading AWS Managed Grafana Installed With Terraform

If you have followed the procedure of [installing Amazon Managed Grafana with Terraform](#grafana_terraform_aws), you can follow these steps to upgrade the dashboards:

1.  Download the latest [dashboard bundle](#dashboard_downloads) and follow the installation procedure as previously using the path of the newly downloaded dashboards.
    

* * *

If you have any questions or need any assistance contact the Develocity support team or your customer success representative.

<a id="appendix"></a>

## Appendix

<a id="disable_old_export"></a>

### Appendix A: Disabling V1.0 Build Model Export

To disable the V1.0 Build Model Export via UI, follow these steps:

1.  Navigate to **Administration**  **Advanced**
    
2.  Select **Delete** for the `feature.buildModelExport=ENABLED` line in **Config parameters**
    
    ![Example of Disabling the v1.0 Build Model Export](https://docs.gradle.com/develocity/reporting-aws/2.1/_images/admin-export.png)
    
    Example of Disabling the v1.0 Build Model Export
    
3.  Select **Save**
    
4.  Follow the instructions to restart the Develocity server
    

If the V1.0 Build Model Export was enabled via unattended configuration, you can disable it by updating the following configuration from the `values.yaml` Helm chart or removing them entirely:

```yaml
app:
  params:
    feature.buildModelExport: DISABLED
# configure here when using a separate bg processor
# appBackgroundProcessor:
#   params:
#     feature.buildModelExport: DISABLED
```

For more information, see the “Unattended configuration” section in the [Develocity Administration Manual for Helm Installations](https://docs.gradle.com/develocity/2026.2/administration/unattended-configuration/).

<a id="dashboard_downloads"></a>

### Appendix B: Dashboard Bundle Downloads

Consider [Develocity version compatibility](https://docs.gradle.com/develocity/2026.1/miscellaneous/compatibility/#develocity-reporting-and-visualization-dashboard-bundles) when choosing which dashboard bundle to download.

*   [Dashboard bundle 1.10.0 ZIP file](https://docs.gradle.com/downloads/dashboards-release-bundle/dashboards-release-bundle-1.10.0.zip) ([SHA256 checksum](https://docs.gradle.com/downloads/dashboards-release-bundle/dashboards-release-bundle-1.10.0.zip.sha256))
    
*   [Dashboard bundle 1.9.1 ZIP file](https://docs.gradle.com/downloads/dashboards-release-bundle/dashboards-release-bundle-1.9.1.zip) ([SHA256 checksum](https://docs.gradle.com/downloads/dashboards-release-bundle/dashboards-release-bundle-1.9.1.zip.sha256))
    
*   [Dashboard bundle 1.8.3 ZIP file](https://docs.gradle.com/downloads/dashboards-release-bundle/dashboards-release-bundle-1.8.3.zip) ([SHA256 checksum](https://docs.gradle.com/downloads/dashboards-release-bundle/dashboards-release-bundle-1.8.3.zip.sha256))
    
*   [Dashboard bundle 1.7.1 ZIP file](https://docs.gradle.com/downloads/dashboards-release-bundle/dashboards-release-bundle-1.7.1.zip) ([SHA256 checksum](https://docs.gradle.com/downloads/dashboards-release-bundle/dashboards-release-bundle-1.7.1.zip.sha256))
    
*   [Dashboard bundle 1.6.3 ZIP file](https://docs.gradle.com/develocity/legacy/reporting-aws/installation-manual/dashboard-bundles-v2/dashboards-release-bundle-1.6.3.zip) ([SHA256 checksum](https://docs.gradle.com/develocity/legacy/reporting-aws/installation-manual/dashboard-bundles-v2/dashboards-release-bundle-1.6.3.zip.sha256))
    
*   [Dashboard bundle 1.5.4 ZIP file](https://docs.gradle.com/develocity/legacy/reporting-aws/installation-manual/dashboard-bundles-v2/dashboards-release-bundle-1.5.4.zip) ([SHA256 checksum](https://docs.gradle.com/develocity/legacy/reporting-aws/installation-manual/dashboard-bundles-v2/dashboards-release-bundle-1.5.4.zip.sha256))
    

The dashboard bundle includes the SQL statements to set up the tables and views in Athena, which are required for the dashboards to work.

The table in [Develocity Compatibility](https://docs.gradle.com/develocity/2026.2/miscellaneous/compatibility/#develocity_reporting_and_visualization_athena_bundle) shows which Athena schema version and dashboard bundle version are compatible with each other.

Once extracted, the dashboard bundle will look like this:

```
/
├─ kustomization.yaml (1)
├─ dashboards/ (2)
│  ├─ 00 - Overview/
│  │  ├─ global-volume.json
│  │  ├─ ...
│  ├─ 10 - Environment/
│  │  ├─ build-tools.json
│  │  ├─ ...
│  ├─ ...
├─ athena/
│  ├─ v1/ (3)
│  │   ├─ ...
│  ├─ v2/
│  │   ├─ ddl/ (4)
│  │   │   ├─ 001-1-pre-internal_build.sql
│  │   │   ├─ 001-2-internal_build.sql
│  │   │   ├─ ...
│  │   ├─ ...
│  ├─ one-off/
│  │   ├─ ddl/ (5)
│  │   │   ├─ 001-1-pre-internal_build.sql
│  │   │   ├─ 001-2-internal_build.sql
│  │   │   ├─ ...
│  │   ├─ ...
│  ├─ ...
```

1. Kustomization file to import the dashboards into a Kubernetes cluster. Optional if not using Helm/Kubernetes to import the dashboards. See importing dashboards via Helm and Kubernetes for more details.
2. Directory containing the JSON files of the dashboards, organized by category. See importing the Gradle-provided dashboards for details.
3. Schema definitions for the V1.0 version. Not used in V2.0, and can be ignored.
4. Schema definitions for Athena for V2.0. See setting up the Athena schema for details.
5. Schema definitions for one-off Athena Data Export. See setting up the Athena schema for details.

<a id="schema-change-history"></a>

#### Schema Change History

<a id="1-10-x"></a>

##### 1.10.x

<a id="added-new-tables-and-views"></a>

###### Added New Tables and Views:

*   `internal_repository_instabilities_per_category`
    
*   `repository_instabilities_per_category`
    

<a id="updated-tables-and-views"></a>

###### Updated Tables and Views:

*   `build`
    
*   `build_summary`
    
*   `internal_build`
    
*   `internal_build_summary`

The partitioning columns have changed for all tables. See the [2025.3 upgrade notes](https://docs.gradle.com/develocity/2025.3/upgrade-uninstall/upgrade/#athena_data_export) for details.

<a id="breaking-column-change"></a>

###### Breaking Column Change

The `build_start_time` column is now an internal partition column. It’s part of the new partitioning schema for all tables and views. It didn’t exist for most tables and views before, except for the following:

*   `gradle_task_summary`
    
*   `maven_goal_summary`
    
*   `unit_execution_summary`
    

Custom queries using `build_start_time` in these tables will need to be updated to use `build_start_timestamp` instead, which has the same data type and meaning as the previous definition.

<a id="1-5-x"></a>

##### 1.5.x

Initial release for V2.0, which introduces a significant enhancement to data export, leveraging the power of the ORC format. This optimized format enables more efficient data storage and substantially boosts query performance.

The ORC format will reduce the storage footprint of build data and dramatically improve Athena’s efficiency by consolidating numerous small files into larger, more manageable units, resulting in savings on network bandwidth and compute resources.

This improvement also translates directly to lower query costs, as the volume of data processed determines these.

<a id="athena_connection"></a>

### Appendix C: Athena Network Connectivity

The Athena Data Export process connects to Amazon Athena over two different ports:

*   Port 443 to connect to the host
    
*   Port 444 to stream the query results
    

If you are experiencing timeouts or connection issues, check your network configuration to ensure that these ports are open and accessible.

For more details refer to the [Amazon Athena documentation](https://repost.aws/knowledge-center/athena-connection-timeout-jdbc-odbc-driver).

<a id="athena_user_managed_schema"></a>

### Appendix D: User-Managed Athena Schema

<a id="using-the-athena-console"></a>

#### Using the Athena Console

The schemas used for the Athena Data Export are provided as part of the dashboard bundle found in [Dashboard bundle downloads](#dashboard_downloads). To apply them, first download the dashboard bundle corresponding to your Develocity version.

The DDL for the tables/views is contained in individual files within `athena/v2/ddl`.

In case you are using the one-off Athena Data Export, they can be found in `athena/one-off/ddl`.

Using the Athena console, you can run the DDL scripts in your Athena database. Since Athena only allows executing one statement at a time, some tables/views have been split into multiple files for convenience.

For first time setup, all the statements in all the files must be run in numerical order.

For later upgrades, it’s sufficient to update only the tables and views that changed, in numerical order. All updates to the schema are described in [Schema change history](#schema-change-history).

> [!NOTE]
> Our Athena tables are created by reading existing data from S3 buckets as external tables, and cannot modify that data. Because of this, dropping the tables and replacing the views won’t result in any data loss, making it safe to run all the statements included in the dashboard bundle.

The bundles contain two placeholders that need to be changed before the statements are executed:

1.  Replace the `${s3.path}` placeholder to point to the S3 location used to save the build models.
    
    In contrast, if you are applying the schemas for the one-off export, it must instead include `athena-data-export`, for example, `s3://develocity/athena-data-export`.+
    
    For the **new synchronized Athena Data Export** use the following script to replace the placeholder in all the files:
    
    By default, the new value needs to include `reporting`, for example, `s3://develocity/reporting/`.
    
    For the **one-off sync** use the following script to replace the placeholder in all the files:
    
    The new value needs to include `athena-data-export` (unless a different prefix was configured), for example, `s3://develocity/athena-data-export`
    
    ```shell
    find ./ddl -type f -name '*.sql' -exec sed -i.bak 's/${s3.path}/YOUR-S3-PATH\//g' {} \; \
      && find ./ddl -type f -name '*.sql.bak' -exec rm {} \;
    ```
    

For each of the individual files in Athena, follow these steps:

1.  Select the database you created in Glue previously.
    
    ![Selecting the database in the Athena console](https://docs.gradle.com/develocity/reporting-aws/2.1/_images/select-table.png)
    
    Example of Selecting the Athena Database
    
2.  In the Query Editor, select **Create** in **Tables and Views**, then select **Create Table**.
    
    ![Creating a new table or view in the Athena Query Editor](https://docs.gradle.com/develocity/reporting-aws/2.1/_images/create-table.png)
    
    Example of Creating a New Table/View
    
3.  Enter the DDL statement for the table/view from the bundle downloaded from [Dashboard and schema bundle downloads](#dashboard_downloads).
    
4.  Select **Run**.
    
5.  Verify that the query was executed successfully. For the first time setup, Athena might report a warning about items missing from the filesystem - this is expected and can be ignored.
    

> [!NOTE]
> The pre and post files (if included) are only required when upgrading. They can be skipped for the first time setup.

See [Creating tables using AWS Glue or the Athena console](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/athena/latest/ug/creating-tables-how-to.html) for more details.

If you have any questions or need any assistance, please contact the Develocity support team. We can provide snippets or resource definitions and their adaptions to any special requirements you may have.

<a id="using-terraform"></a>

#### Using Terraform

If you use Terraform to manage your AWS resources, we provide a set of Terraform modules and scripts alongside the dashboard bundle to create and populate an Athena workgroup and the required tables.

When creating the tables using Terraform, there are a few caveats to consider.

<a id="views"></a>

##### Views

The AWS terraform resources don’t support creating Athena views out of the box. [This repository](https://github.com/iconara/terraform-aws-athena-view) provides the possibility to create Athena views with some workarounds.

<a id="column-types"></a>

##### Column Types

For Athena views and tables, it’s required that the terraform resource has all column types explicitly defined for all tables and views. A mismatch between the column types of the views and their respective tables will cause the data export not to work.

<a id="column-order"></a>

##### Column Order

The Athena views expose many fields nested in different structures of the exported build models. **The field order defined in Terraform and in the views must match**. If there is a mismatch, the data will be attributed to the wrong column, leading to incorrect results or errors in the dashboards.

<a id="v1_upgrade_guide"></a>

### Appendix E: Upgrading From V1.0

The V2.0 Athena Data Export and the V1.0 Build Model Export work entirely independently and have different data formats. Existing build model data stored in the V1.0 format cannot be viewed in the V2.0 format. Likewise, data exported in the V2.0 format cannot be viewed in the V1.0 format.

> [!TIP]
> The two processes can be run in parallel, but it’s recommended to disable the V1.0 Build Model Export entirely once data parity is achieved. See [Appendix A](#disable_old_export) for details on how to disable the V1.0 export process.

Upgrading from V1.0 requires a complete new setup, so please follow the steps detailed in the [Setup](#setup) guide.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> The following two changes must be noted when upgrading from V1.0

When creating the [Athena database](#configure_aws_glue), note that the database name must be different from the one used in the previous setup to avoid collisions.

When upgrading, you can skip [setting up a new workgroup](#create_athena_workgroup), these can be reused between versions

<a id="upgrade_guide_2_0"></a>

### Appendix F: Changes After 2025.3

In the 2025.3 release the Athena Data Export process was re-implemented to provide a more robust and scalable solution. This new implementation is used by default when installing or upgrading to 2025.3 or later. The new implementation constantly _synchronizes_ the exported Build Models with Develocity, thus providing a consistent view at all times. This allows us to keep adding new data and not have to rely on re-running the export process manually. In this documentation we will refer to this new engine as "**synchronized Athena Data Export**" and the old implementation as "**one-off Athena Data Export**".

Build data exported from Develocity will now be subject to the configured retention period and will be directed to a new location within the designated S3 bucket. It’s important to note that previously exported build data won’t be migrated. Instead, Develocity will initiate a fresh export of all currently retained builds to the new location. This re-export process may be time-consuming and could temporarily strain your Develocity instance until all historical builds have been caught up. Develocity will automatically update the schema definitions of your Glue database to reflect the new S3 location, which will necessitate additional permissions in the attached IAM policy. While this new data export mechanism is the default, Develocity offers configuration options to facilitate a smooth transition. Users have the choice to continue using the existing export method or to configure a second Glue database, allowing the existing export mechanism to run in parallel with the new one until the transition is complete.

<a id="maintaining-data-availability-throughout-the-upgrade"></a>

#### Maintaining Data Availability Throughout the Upgrade

As explained above, the new synchronized Athena Data Export needs to re-export all historical builds that are still retained in Develocity. This can take a significant amount of time depending on the number of builds that need to be exported. During this time, the data shown in the dashboards will be incomplete. To avoid this situation, you can choose to run both the new synchronized Athena Data Export and the legacy one-off Athena Data Export in parallel until the re-export is complete.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> The settings to enable the one-off Athena Data Export are temporary and will be removed in Develocity 2026.1.

```yaml
athenaDataExport:
  enabled: true
  exportType: both (1)
  oneOffExportDatabase: $LEGACY_DATABASE (2)
```

1. Set to both to enable both the new and old export processes.
2. When both export processes are enabled, this must be set to the name of the Glue database used by the old export process. Note that in the case where both processes are enabled they need to run against different Glue databases. Please note the limitation of the automatic schema management when both export processes are enabled as described in Automatic Schema Management.

The new Athena Data Export Engine can also be disabled entirely by setting the following in your `values.yaml`:

```yaml
athenaDataExport:
  enabled: true
  schemaManagement:
    enabled: false (1)
  exportType: oneOff (2)
```

1. Since one-off export isn’t supported with automatic schema management, this must be set to false.
2. Set to oneOff to only enable the legacy Athena Data Export. Please note the limitation of the automatic schema management when one-off export is enabled as described in Automatic Schema Management.

<a id="data_discrepancy"></a>

### Appendix G: Discrepancy in Data Between Athena and Develocity

In certain situations, you may find that queries made to Athena or the provided dashboards show different numbers than the Develocity UI. Most notably, the _Build count_ metric on the _Global Volume_ dashboard might not match the number of builds shown in Develocity’s scan list page for the same time range.

A few factors can cause this discrepancy:

*   Build synchronization from Develocity to Athena isn’t instantaneous. The build data is periodically queued for synchronization. Recent builds may take up to 10 minutes to be queued. The time for the build to appear after that depends on the level of build traffic the Develocity instance experiences. Depending on build traffic, it can take up to 30 minutes for the most recent data to appear in Athena. If it takes longer than that, then there may be a problem, so contact Gradle support.
    
*   Builds with a start date older than the last 24 hours (as measured by the Athena Data Export in the UTC timezone) may take up to a day after their end date to appear in Athena. The Athena Data Export scans the last 24 hours very frequently for new or modified builds that started within that time frame, but older time ranges are only scanned daily. Builds that started outside the 24-hour window will only appear in Athena in the first daily scan after the build’s end date. Depending on the start time of the build, this would only potentially affect very-long-running builds that have runtimes approaching 24 hours.
    
*   The queries in the dashboards discard the 'time' part of the dates selected in the date picker and work only on the dates. In addition, the dates are converted to UTC before being sent to the query engine. If a non-UTC timezone is used when selecting the dates in Grafana, this can spill over into the previous or next day, and query results unexpectedly contain a full extra day of data.
    

<a id="aws_limits"></a>

### Appendix H: Amazon Athena Rate Limiting

Amazon Athena enforces rate limits on the number of requests that can be made to the service within a certain time frame. Under high load, it’s possible that Athena throttles requests, resulting in failed queries or delayed data updates with error messages similar to: `Could not load query results: software.amazon.awssdk.services.athenastreaming.model.AthenaStreamingException: Rate exceeded`

In the unlikely scenario that you encounter such rate limiting issues on a regular basis, consider reaching out to AWS support to request an increase in your Athena service limits for the following APIs:

*   GetQueryResults API
    
*   StartQueryExecution API
    
*   GetQueryExecution API
    

More details can be found in the [Amazon Athena documentation](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/athena/latest/ug/service-limits.html).

# Develocity IntelliJ Plugin User Manual

<a id="preamble"></a>

The [Develocity IntelliJ plugin](https://plugins.jetbrains.com/plugin/27471-develocity) seamlessly integrates Develocity and Build Scan capabilities directly into your IDE.

*   It displays a [live build timeline](#live_build_timeline) of task/goal execution and resource usage within your IntelliJ IDE, for all your Gradle and Maven builds.
    
*   It can automatically configure your Gradle build to [publish Build Scans](#build_scan_publication) to gradle.com or your Develocity server.
    
*   It decorates your Java/Kotlin/Groovy test source files with [historical test results](#test_history).
    

<a id="features"></a>

## Features

<a id="live_build_timeline"></a>

### Live Build Timeline

_Available for: All Users_

The plugin displays a live timeline of task/goal execution and resource usage within the IntelliJ Run tool window. This helps identify bottlenecks and visualize parallelism.

Run a Gradle or Maven build (e.g., via Run Configuration or Gradle Sync). The timeline appears in the build output window.

<a id="tabs-1"></a>

Live build timeline

*   <a id="tabs-1-gradle"></a>
    
    Gradle
    
*   <a id="tabs-1-maven"></a>
    
    Maven
    

<a id="tabs-1-gradle--panel"></a>

![Live Gradle build timeline](https://docs.gradle.com/develocity/intellij-plugin/1.3/_images/intellij-timeline-gradle.gif)

Live build timeline

<a id="tabs-1-maven--panel"></a>

![Live Maven build timeline](https://docs.gradle.com/develocity/intellij-plugin/1.3/_images/intellij-timeline-maven.gif)

Live build timeline

> [!TIP]
> Hover over blocks to see task/goal duration and type.

> [!TIP]
> CPU and Memory resource usage is visible while the build runs.

<a id="build_scan_publication"></a>

### Build Scan Publication

_Available for: Users publishing to gradle.com or users with a Develocity server_

The plugin can automatically configure your Gradle build to publish Build Scans to gradle.com or your Develocity server.

When a Build Scan is published, a notification with a link to the Build Scan appears in the IDE, and you can also access the Build Scan from the timeline toolbar and task/goal details.

![Accessing the published Build Scan](https://docs.gradle.com/develocity/intellij-plugin/1.3/_images/build-scan-access.png)

Accessing the published Build Scan

> [!NOTE]
> To learn more about Build Scans, see [https://scans.gradle.com](https://scans.gradle.com).

<a id="test_history"></a>

### Test History

_Available for: Users connected to a Develocity Server with the Test Analytics feature enabled_

When connected to a Develocity server, the plugin decorates your Java/Kotlin/Groovy test source files with historical results. By default, all Build Scans published to your Develocity server (i.e. from you or other local users, and from CI agents) contribute to this analysis. You can use [query patterns](#query_patterns) to scope the data to specific builds.

Test class and test methods are decorated with inlays showing recent pass/fail/flakiness history.

![Test history](https://docs.gradle.com/develocity/intellij-plugin/1.3/_images/test-history.png)

Test history

> [!NOTE]
> Test history requires permission to access the Develocity Test API. The provided access key must have the [`Access build data via the API` permission](https://docs.gradle.com/develocity/2026.2/administration/access-control/permissions-and-roles/#permissions).

> [!TIP]
> Test history can be configured via the settings to work with data from the past day, or the past 7 days.

<a id="query_patterns"></a>

#### Query Patterns

By default, test history includes data from all builds published to your Develocity server. Query patterns let you define named filters to scope which builds contribute to the test history analysis.

For example, you might create a pattern that only includes CI builds, or one that focuses on builds from a specific branch.

Query patterns are managed in the plugin settings. Each pattern has a name and a filter expression using the [Develocity search syntax](https://docs.gradle.com/develocity/2026.2/reference/develocity-api/#advanced-search-syntax). A built-in "All builds" pattern is always available and includes all builds without filtering.

![Query patterns in the plugin settings](https://docs.gradle.com/develocity/intellij-plugin/1.3/_images/query-patterns.png)

Query patterns in the plugin settings

By default, all terms in a filter must match. Terms can be combined using boolean `and` and `or` operators, grouped using parentheses, and negated using `-` or `not`.

Example query patterns  
| Name | Filter |
| --- | --- |
| CI builds only | tag:CI |
| My builds on CI | tag:CI user:${user} |
| My branch | value:"Git branch=${currentBranch}" |
| Local or custom tag | tag:local or tag:foo |
| CI on a specific project | project:my-project tag:CI |

The active query pattern is shown in the IDE status bar. Click the status bar widget to quickly switch between patterns.

![Status bar widget for switching query patterns](https://docs.gradle.com/develocity/intellij-plugin/1.3/_images/status-bar-widget.png)

Status bar widget for switching query patterns

<a id="placeholders"></a>

##### Placeholders

Filter expressions support the following placeholders, which are resolved dynamically:

 
| Placeholder | Description |
| --- | --- |
| ${currentBranch} | Resolves to the name of the current Git branch of the open project. Only Git is currently supported; if the branch can’t be determined (for example, the project isn’t a Git repository), any filter clause containing this placeholder is silently removed. |
| ${user} | Resolves to the current operating system user name. |

<a id="installation"></a>

## Installation

*   Open IntelliJ IDEA.
    
*   Go to **File**  **Settings** (or **IntelliJ IDEA**  **Settings** on macOS).
    
*   Navigate to **Plugins**.
    
*   Select the **Marketplace** tab.
    
*   Search for "Develocity".
    
*   Click **Install** next to the "Develocity" plugin and restart your IDE when prompted.
    

![Plugin Installation](https://docs.gradle.com/develocity/intellij-plugin/1.3/_images/marketplace.png)

Plugin Installation

<a id="getting_started"></a>

## Getting Started

Choose the setup path that best matches your environment.

<a id="path_local"></a>

### Path A: Standalone (Local)

_For users who want local build insights without connecting to a Develocity server._

You can benefit from the [live build timeline](#live_build_timeline) feature:

1.  Open the settings via **File**  **Settings**  **Tools**  **Develocity** (or **IntelliJ IDEA**  **Settings**  **Tools**  **Develocity** on macOS).
    
2.  Set **Develocity Connection** to `None`.
    
3.  Ensure the `Live build timeline` feature is selected.
    
4.  To see the live build timeline, your build needs to be configured:
    
    *   **Gradle:** Select the `Configure the build` and `Apply Develocity Gradle plugin` checkboxes to configure it automatically.
        
    *   **Maven:** You must manually add the Develocity Maven extension. See the [Develocity Maven Extension User Manual](https://docs.gradle.com/develocity/maven/2.5/maven-extension/#manual-setup).
        
    

⇒ Your next build will now show a live timeline while executing.

<a id="tabs-2"></a>

Live build timeline

*   <a id="tabs-2-gradle"></a>
    
    Gradle
    
*   <a id="tabs-2-maven"></a>
    
    Maven
    

<a id="tabs-2-gradle--panel"></a>

![Live build timeline](https://docs.gradle.com/develocity/intellij-plugin/1.3/_images/intellij-timeline-gradle.gif)

Live build timeline

<a id="tabs-2-maven--panel"></a>

![Live build timeline](https://docs.gradle.com/develocity/intellij-plugin/1.3/_images/intellij-timeline-maven.gif)

Live build timeline

<a id="path_gradle_com"></a>

### Path B: Connected (gradle.com)

_For users who want deep build insights using the free Build Scan service._

In addition to the [live build timeline](#live_build_timeline) mentioned above, you can decide to [publish a free Build Scan](#build_scan_publication) to gradle.com for deeper insights into your build.

> [!NOTE]
> To learn more about Build Scans, see [https://scans.gradle.com](https://scans.gradle.com).

To publish Build Scans to gradle.com:

1.  Open the settings via **File**  **Settings**  **Tools**  **Develocity** (or **IntelliJ IDEA**  **Settings**  **Tools**  **Develocity** on macOS).
    
2.  Set **Develocity Connection** to `Develocity at gradle.com`.
    
3.  Configure your build to accept the [Gradle Terms of Use](https://gradle.com/help/legal-terms-of-use):
    
    *   **Gradle:** Select the `Configure the build` and `I agree to the Gradle Terms of Use` checkboxes.
        
    *   **Maven:** You must manually add the Develocity Maven extension and accept the Terms of Use. See the [Develocity Maven Extension User Manual](https://docs.gradle.com/develocity/maven/2.5/maven-extension/#accept-the-scans-gradle-com-terms-of-use).
        
    

⇒ Your next build will now publish a Build Scan to gradle.com when it completes, and a notification with a link to the Build Scan will appear in the IDE.

![Accessing the published Build Scan](https://docs.gradle.com/develocity/intellij-plugin/1.3/_images/build-scan-access.png)

Accessing the published Build Scan

<a id="path_develocity"></a>

### Path C: Connecting with a Develocity Server

_For users with access to a Develocity server._

If your organization uses Develocity, connecting the plugin unlocks [historical test results](#test_history), in addition to the [live build timeline](#live_build_timeline) and [automatic Build Scan publishing](#build_scan_publication) features mentioned above.

1.  Open the settings via **File**  **Settings**  **Tools**  **Develocity** (or **IntelliJ IDEA**  **Settings…​** on macOS).
    
2.  Set **Develocity Connection** to `Develocity server`.
    
3.  Enter your **Develocity Server URL**.
    
4.  Authenticate with your credentials, if needed:
    
    *   Click the **Log in…​** button.
        
    *   Authentication can be auto-discovered based on existing configuration files on your machine, or a known access key can be provided or generated via your browser.
        
    *   _Authentication is required to access Test History features._
        
    
5.  Ensure the `Test history in source files` feature is selected.
    

⇒ Test history will be available in your Java/Kotlin/Groovy test source files.

![Test history](https://docs.gradle.com/develocity/intellij-plugin/1.3/_images/test-history.png)

Test history

<a id="configuration-reference"></a>

## Configuration Reference

Configuration is managed via **File**  **Settings**  **Tools**  **Develocity** (or **IntelliJ IDEA**  **Settings**  **Tools**  **Develocity** on macOS).

![Develocity Configuration](https://docs.gradle.com/develocity/intellij-plugin/1.3/_images/intellij-develocity-configuration.png)

Develocity Configuration

 
| Develocity Connection | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Develocity Server | Select this option when connecting to a Develocity server (e.g. your organization’s Develocity server). URL: Specify the URL of your Develocity server (e.g., https://develocity.example.com). Log in…​: Specify the access key to be used to authenticate with the Develocity server. Required for the Test History feature. Allow untrusted server: Enables connecting to Develocity servers with self-signed or untrusted SSL certificates. |
| Develocity at gradle.com | Select this option when connecting to the free Develocity service at gradle.com. |
| None | Select this option when not connecting to any Develocity server (local-only usage). |

 
| Features | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Live build timeline | Enables the live build timeline feature for Gradle and Maven builds executed within IntelliJ. Requires the Develocity Gradle plugin (4.1+) or Develocity Maven extension (2.2.1+). For Gradle builds, the Develocity Gradle plugin can be auto-applied to your build. |
| Test history in source files | Enables test history in Java/Kotlin/Groovy test source files. Requires connection to a Develocity server with the Test Analytics feature enabled. A time range for the test history data can be specified (past day or past 7 days). Query patterns can be defined to filter which builds contribute to the test history analysis. Patterns use the Develocity search syntax and support dynamic placeholders like ${currentBranch} and ${user}. |

<a id="gradle_build"></a>

 
| Gradle build | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Configure the build | Automatically configures your Gradle build without modifying its Gradle files. Apply Develocity Gradle plugin: Specify the Develocity Gradle plugin to be used. When configured, the Develocity server URL is also passed to the build and will take precedence over any in-build configuration. |

 
| Maven build | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Configure the build | Automatically configuring your Maven build is currently not supported. You will need to manually add the Develocity Maven extension to your build. See the Develocity Maven Extension User Manual for instructions. |

<a id="troubleshooting"></a>

## Troubleshooting

<a id="live-build-timeline-shows-no-data"></a>

### Live Build Timeline Shows No Data

**Symptom** — The timeline view displays a message like "Something went wrong and no data was received from the build."

**Cause** — The Develocity IntelliJ plugin isn’t receiving data from the Develocity Gradle plugin / Develocity Maven extension. This typically happens if the Gradle plugin / Maven extension version applied to your build is older than the minimum required version.

**Solution** — Ensure your build applies Develocity Gradle plugin 4.1 or newer, or Develocity Maven extension 2.2.1 or newer.

<a id="some-of-my-maven-builds-arent-shown-in-the-live-build-timeline"></a>

### Some of My Maven Builds Aren’t Shown in the Live Build Timeline

**Symptom** — The timeline view isn’t displayed for some Maven builds.

**Cause** — The build isn’t delegating to Maven, but uses the internal IDE build mechanism. For instance Maven sync/reload aren’t delegating to Maven, or the IDE can be configured to run tests without delegating to Maven.

**Solution** — Configure your IDE to delegate the build/test actions to Maven, or don’t expect the timeline view to be shown for such builds.

<a id="live-build-timeline-is-affecting-the-performance-of-my-machine"></a>

### Live Build Timeline Is Affecting the Performance of My Machine

**Symptom** — CPU usage spikes when the timeline view is visible.

**Cause** — The timeline view might repaint too frequently for the capabilities of your machine.

**Solution** — Go to **Help**  **Find Action**, type `Registry` and press Enter to open the IDE registry. Then look for the key `com.gradle.develocity.ide.timeline.refresh.millis`. You can specify any value between 10ms and 5000ms. Try a bigger value to reduce the performance impact of the timeline view.

<a id="connection-to-develocity-server-fails"></a>

### Connection to Develocity Server Fails

**Symptom** — The settings page displays a message like "Connection to Develocity failed".

**Cause** — The Develocity server URL is incorrect, or there is a network issue preventing the connection.

**Solution** — Verify the Develocity server URL is correct, and that your machine can reach the server.

<a id="connection-to-develocity-server-indicates-no-api-access"></a>

### Connection to Develocity Server Indicates "no API access"

**Symptom** — The settings page displays a message like "Connection to Develocity OK (without API access)".

**Cause** — No access key was automatically discovered or provided.

**Solution** — Click the **Log in…​** button and provide a valid access key with the `Access build data via the API` permission.

<a id="connection-to-develocity-test-api-fails"></a>

### Connection to Develocity Test API Fails

**Symptom** — The settings page displays a message like "Connection to Develocity Test API failed".

**Cause** — The provided access key doesn’t have the `Access build data via the API` permission, or the Develocity server doesn’t have the Test Analytics feature enabled.

**Solution** — Provide an access key with the `Access build data via the API` permission, or contact your Develocity server administrator to enable the Test Analytics feature.

# Develocity CLI (develocityctl)

<a id="preamble"></a>

Use the `develocityctl` command line tool to manage your Develocity instance. It can perform tasks related to your instance, some of which require a connection to the instance.

<a id="supported-develocity-versions"></a>

## Supported Develocity Versions

Supported Develocity Server Versions 
| Develocity Server Version |
| --- |
| 2024.3 - 2026.2.0 |

<a id="installation"></a>

## Installation

Install `develocityctl` by following the instructions in the [installation guide](https://docs.gradle.com/develocity/develocityctl/1.23/install/).

You can choose one of the following installation methods:

*   [Use the JAR file](https://docs.gradle.com/develocity/develocityctl/1.23/install/#installing-the-jar-file).
    
*   [Use the Docker image](https://docs.gradle.com/develocity/develocityctl/1.23/install/#installing-the-develocityctl-docker-image).
    

<a id="using-develocityctl"></a>

## Using develocityctl

You can use `develocityctl` to perform various tasks, such as backing up your database, managing configuration files, and interacting with the Develocity system.

[Overview of `develocityctl` commands](https://docs.gradle.com/develocity/develocityctl/1.23/commands/).

<a id="download"></a>

### Download

<a id="jar_downloads"></a>

#### JAR

You can download the latest version of the `develocityctl` JAR file and its associated files from the following links:

*   [JAR file](https://docs.gradle.com/downloads/develocityctl/develocityctl-1.23.0.jar)
    
*   [JAR file SHA256 checksum](https://docs.gradle.com/downloads/develocityctl/develocityctl-1.23.0.jar.sha256)
    
*   [JAR file PGP signature](https://docs.gradle.com/downloads/develocityctl/develocityctl-1.23.0.jar.asc)
    
*   [JAR file PGP signature SHA256 checksum](https://docs.gradle.com/downloads/develocityctl/develocityctl-1.23.0.jar.asc.sha256)
    

```shell
curl -L -o develocityctl.jar https://docs.gradle.com/downloads/develocityctl/develocityctl-1.23.0.jar
```

<a id="docker"></a>

#### Docker

```shell
docker pull gradle/develocityctl:1.23.0
```
